lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Ore extraction is the heart of your gold mining operation. It is the physical work of breaking gold-bearing rock from the ground and getting it to the surface. If you extract too little, you waste time and money. If you extract too much waste rock, you waste effort on processing material that has no gold. The goal is to extract ore efficiently and handle it carefully so that no gold is lost. In artisanal mining, most gold is fine particles locked in quartz veins or alluvial gravel. You need to break the rock and move it without scattering the gold. Poor extraction and handling can lose up to 30% of your gold before you even start processing.

In Africa, artisanal miners often work in remote areas with limited equipment. You might be using hand tools like picks, shovels, and hammers, or you might have a small jaw crusher or stamp mill. The methods you choose depend on your deposit type. For hard rock, you drill and blast or use manual methods to break the ore. For alluvial deposits, you dig and wash gravel. Handling includes loading, transporting, and stockpiling ore. Each step must be done with care to prevent gold loss. For example, when you blast, fine gold can fly away with dust. When you transport, spillage can occur. When you stockpile, rain can wash away fine gold.

This module will teach you practical techniques to extract and handle ore effectively. You will learn the tools you need, step-by-step methods, common mistakes, and safety practices. By the end, you will be able to run a more productive and profitable operation. Remember, gold is heavy and does not travel far on its own, but careless handling can move it away from you. Every gram counts. In artisanal mining, a gram of gold can be worth a day's wage. So treat your ore like the treasure it is.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To extract and handle ore efficiently, you need the right tools. For hard rock mining, you will need a pickaxe, sledgehammer, chisel, and crowbar. A pickaxe with a sharp point breaks rock, while a sledgehammer (4-8 kg) is for driving chisels or breaking large boulders. Chisels should be made of hardened steel, about 30 cm long, and you need several sizes. A crowbar (1.5 m) helps lever out loose rock. For drilling, you can use a hand drill (star drill) or a manual auger. If you have access to a compressor and jackhammer, that speeds up work, but many artisanal miners start with hand tools.

For alluvial mining, you need a shovel, pick, and a pan or sluice box. A good shovel with a long handle saves your back. A pick breaks compacted gravel. You also need buckets (20 L) to carry gravel, and a wheelbarrow or sacks for transport. For hauling ore from underground, a wheelbarrow or a small cart on rails is useful. If you work underground, you need a headlamp or torch, and a rope for hauling buckets up shafts.

Safety gear is essential: hard hat, safety glasses, gloves, steel-toed boots, and dust mask. In Africa, many miners skip these, but they prevent injuries. You also need a first aid kit. For processing, you will need a mortar and pestle or a stamp mill to crush ore, and a pan for panning. A sluice box with riffles captures fine gold. You can build one with wood and carpet. Always have a tarp to catch spills when handling ore. A magnet helps remove iron particles. Finally, a notebook to record where you extracted ore and how much gold you recovered. This helps you improve.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Step 1: Identify the ore body. Look for quartz veins in rock or pay streaks in gravel. Test pan a sample to confirm gold. Mark the area with stakes. Step 2: Remove overburden. Clear soil, vegetation, and waste rock. Pile it away from your working area. Step 3: Break the ore. For hard rock, drill holes along the vein using a chisel and hammer. Space holes 30-50 cm apart. Fill with explosives if you have them, or use feathers and wedges to split rock. For manual breaking, hit the rock along natural cracks. Aim to produce pieces 10-20 cm across. Step 4: Reduce size. Use a sledgehammer to break larger pieces into smaller ones (5-10 cm). This makes transport easier. Step 5: Load ore. Use shovels and buckets to load ore into wheelbarrows or sacks. Do not mix waste rock with ore. Step 6: Transport. Move ore to your processing site. If underground, haul buckets up shafts with a rope and pulley. Use a cart if possible. Step 7: Stockpile. Place ore on a concrete pad or tarpaulin. Keep different grades separate (high-grade, low-grade). Cover with a tarp to protect from rain. Step 8: Crush and process. Crush ore to sand size using a stamp mill or mortar. Then pan or sluice to recover gold. Step 9: Clean up. Sweep the area and collect any spilled material. Pan the sweepings to recover fine gold. Step 10: Record. Note how much ore you extracted, where, and how much gold you got. This helps you plan next time. Remember, the goal is to extract only ore, not waste, and to handle it gently to avoid losing gold.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Extracting too much waste rock. Many miners break everything, hoping to find gold. This wastes time and processing capacity. Fix: Sample and test before extracting. Only break rock that shows gold or is near gold-bearing veins. Mistake 2: Losing fine gold during blasting. Explosives can blow fine gold into the air. Fix: Use smaller charges, cover the blast area with mats, and collect dust. Mistake 3: Spilling ore during transport. Carrying ore in open buckets or sacks can spill. Fix: Use closed containers or tie sacks securely. Place a tarp under loading areas. Mistake 4: Mixing high-grade and low-grade ore. This dilutes your high-grade and lowers recovery. Fix: Keep grades separate. Use different stockpiles and label them. Mistake 5: Stockpiling on bare ground. Gold particles can sink into soil or wash away. Fix: Build a concrete pad or use a thick tarpaulin. Cover with a roof or tarp. Mistake 6: Not crushing fine enough. If ore is too coarse, gold remains locked in rock. Fix: Crush to at least 2 mm (sand size). Use a stamp mill or ball mill if available. Mistake 7: Ignoring safety. Accidents stop work. Fix: Wear protective gear, support underground workings, and never work alone. Mistake 8: Not recording data. Without records, you cannot improve. Fix: Keep a logbook of extraction and recovery. Mistake 9: Using wrong tools. Using a pick on hard rock instead of a sledgehammer wastes energy. Fix: Match tools to the job. Mistake 10: Skipping cleanup. Gold dust settles on floors and equipment. Fix: Regularly sweep and pan cleanup material. Each fix is simple but can increase your gold recovery by 10-20%.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety is not optional. Mining is dangerous. In Africa, many accidents happen because miners take shortcuts. Always wear a hard hat, safety glasses, gloves, steel-toed boots, and a dust mask. Dust from crushing ore contains silica, which causes lung disease. Wet the ore before crushing to reduce dust. If you work underground, never go alone. Use wooden or steel supports to prevent cave-ins. Check the roof for loose rock before starting. Use a rope and harness when working in shafts. Ensure good ventilation. Use a canary or gas detector if you suspect bad air. For blasting, use only licensed explosives and follow safety rules. Keep bystanders away. Never relight a misfire immediately; wait 30 minutes. When handling ore, use proper lifting techniques. Bend your knees, not your back. Don't overload wheelbarrows. Keep your work area tidy to avoid trips and falls. Store tools safely. Have a first aid kit and know how to use it. Best practices include: plan your work, communicate with your team, and take breaks. Drink water to avoid heat exhaustion. In hot climates, work early morning or late afternoon. Maintain your tools; a dull chisel is more dangerous than a sharp one. Finally, respect the environment. Do not dump waste into rivers. Rehabilitate mined areas. Use mercury responsibly or avoid it altogether. By following these practices, you protect yourself, your team, and your community.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice. This exercise will help you apply what you learned. You will need: a pickaxe, shovel, sledgehammer, chisel, buckets, wheelbarrow, tarpaulin, and a pan. Choose a small area with visible quartz veins or alluvial gravel. If you have a known gold-bearing spot, use that. Otherwise, test pan a few samples to find a good spot. Mark a 2m x 2m square. Remove overburden and set it aside. Dig or break the ore within the square. For hard rock, drill a few holes with a chisel and hammer, then break the rock with a sledgehammer. Aim for pieces 10-20 cm. For alluvial, dig gravel and pick out large rocks. Load all ore into buckets and carry to a tarpaulin. Weigh or estimate the volume. Crush a sample of ore to sand size using a mortar and pestle. Pan the crushed ore carefully. Count the gold particles or weigh the gold. Record your results: area, volume, and gold recovered. Now, repeat the process but with better handling: cover the ore with a tarp when transporting, keep high-grade separate, and sweep the area after. Compare gold recovery. You should see an improvement. Finally, clean up your site. Fill the hole, replace overburden, and dispose of waste properly. Write a short report: what worked, what didn't, and what you will do differently. This exercise teaches you the value of careful extraction and handling. Do it regularly to improve your skills.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of ore extraction?
options: A) To extract as much rock as possible
B) To extract ore efficiently without losing gold
C) To extract only waste rock
D) To extract gold directly from the ground
quiz.explanation: The goal is to extract ore efficiently and handle it carefully to avoid gold loss.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for breaking hard rock in artisanal mining?
quiz.explanation: A sledgehammer is used for breaking hard rock and driving chisels.

quiz.q: Why should you keep high-grade and low-grade ore separate?
options: B) To avoid diluting high-grade ore
quiz.explanation: Mixing high-grade with low-grade dilutes the high-grade and lowers overall recovery.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake during blasting?
options: B) Losing fine gold in dust
quiz.explanation: Blasting can blow fine gold into the air, causing loss.

quiz.q: What should you do before extracting ore?
options: B) Sample and test the rock
quiz.explanation: Sampling and testing confirm whether the rock contains gold before extraction.

quiz.q: Which safety gear is essential when crushing ore?
quiz.explanation: All are essential: hard hat, dust mask, and safety glasses protect against injury and dust.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for ore pieces after initial breaking?
quiz.explanation: Ore pieces of 10-20 cm are manageable for transport and further crushing.

quiz.q: Why should you cover stockpiled ore?
options: B) To prevent rain from washing away fine gold
C) To hide it from thieves
D) To make it easier to crush
quiz.explanation: Rain can wash away fine gold particles from uncovered stockpiles.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when transporting ore?
options: B) Spill some to lighten load
C) Use closed containers or tie sacks
D) Transport quickly to avoid theft
quiz.explanation: Closed containers or tied sacks prevent spillage and gold loss.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing extraction?
options: A) Leave the site as is
B) Fill the hole and replace overburden
C) Dump waste in a river
D) Start a new hole nearby
quiz.explanation: Rehabilitating the site prevents environmental damage and is a best practice.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety risk in underground mining?
quiz.explanation: Cave-ins are a major risk; proper supports are needed to prevent them.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sluice box?
quiz.explanation: A sluice box with riffles captures fine gold from crushed ore.

quiz.q: How can you reduce dust when crushing ore?
options: D) Work in a closed room
quiz.explanation: Wetting the ore before crushing reduces dust and protects lungs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a misfire after blasting?
quiz.explanation: Waiting 30 minutes reduces the risk of accidental explosion.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important?
quiz.explanation: Records help you track recovery and improve your methods.

quiz.q: What is a recommended tool for drilling holes in hard rock?
quiz.explanation: A chisel and hammer are used for manual drilling in hard rock.

quiz.q: What should be done with spilled ore during handling?
quiz.explanation: Spilled ore may contain fine gold; sweep and pan it to recover gold.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for stockpiling ore?
options: B) On a concrete pad or tarpaulin
quiz.explanation: A concrete pad or tarpaulin prevents gold from sinking into soil.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of silica dust?
quiz.explanation: Silica dust can cause silicosis, a serious lung disease.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting work underground?
quiz.explanation: Checking for loose rock helps prevent cave-ins and accidents.

quiz.q: Why is it important to crush ore to sand size?
options: A) To make it easier to transport
D) To make it look nice
quiz.explanation: Crushing to sand size liberates gold particles for recovery.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test for gold before extraction?
quiz.explanation: Panning a sample is a reliable way to confirm gold presence.

quiz.q: What should you wear when working in a dusty environment?
quiz.explanation: A dust mask protects your lungs from harmful dust.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a wheelbarrow?
quiz.explanation: A wheelbarrow helps transport ore with less effort.

quiz.q: What should you do with waste rock?
options: B) Pile away from working area
quiz.explanation: Waste rock should be piled away to avoid mixing with ore.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work with a team underground?
options: B) For safety and help in emergencies
quiz.explanation: Working with a team ensures someone can get help if an accident occurs.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when stockpiling ore?
quiz.explanation: Placing ore on bare ground can lead to gold loss into the soil.

quiz.q: What should you do after a day of mining?
options: B) Clean up and store tools
quiz.explanation: Cleaning up and storing tools prevents accidents and tool damage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a first aid kit?
quiz.explanation: A first aid kit is for treating injuries promptly.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when breaking ore manually?
quiz.explanation: Hitting along natural cracks makes breaking easier and more efficient.
